problem: "a 0.5 s setup twice" is unclear: it can be read as two setups of 0.5 s each. What the worked example actually charges is 0.5 s setup plus 0.5 s teardown, 1 s in all.
fix: "A short 1 MB file needs only 8 s of data time; 0.5 s of setup plus 0.5 s of teardown is about 1 s on top of that."

problem: "Packet switching wins here because setup dominates" overstates the numbers. Setup plus teardown is 1 s of the 9 s circuit total, roughly 11 percent, and packet switching wins by only about 0.98 s. A student may quote "setup dominates" for a 1 MB file at 1 Mbps, which the arithmetic does not support.
fix: "Packet switching wins here, but only by about 1 s, because the 1 s of setup and teardown is a visible part of this short transfer. For a longer transfer the same 1 s becomes negligible."

where: Section 2, first paragraph, and Quiz Q7
problem: "Each packet carries a header with ... a sequence number" and "A sequence number in the header" are imprecise for IP. The IP header has no sequence number; ordering is done by a sequence number in the transport header (TCP), and UDP has none.
fix: "In a datagram network such as IP, the network header carries the addresses and error checks; a sequence number used to restore order is added by the transport protocol, as TCP does."

problem: The packet lane shows four back-to-back 3 s packets on a single link and ends at 12 s, so the figure shows no store-and-forward delay across hops even though the aria text says the packet lane pays per-packet store-and-forward. A reader may conclude packet switching never adds hop delay.
fix: Add to the caption: "The packet lane shows a single link; over k links each packet also waits for store-and-forward at the intermediate routers, as Worked example 1 counts with the 2 extra hops."
